body:
The coast as a changing landscape

A coast is the zone where land meets the sea. It is one of the most dynamic parts of the Earth's surface because marine processes interact continuously with rocks, sediments, rivers, winds and movements of the Earth's crust.

Coastal landforms develop through 3 principal processes:

  • Erosion: Removal of rock and sediment from the coast.
  • Transportation: Movement of eroded material by waves and currents.
  • Deposition: Accumulation of sediment when transporting energy decreases.

These processes are interconnected. Material removed from one coastal location may subsequently build a beach or another depositional feature elsewhere.

Movements of seawater

MovementPrincipal causeGeomorphic significance
WavesMainly wind blowing over waterErosion, sediment transportation and deposition
TidesGravitational attraction of the Moon and SunPeriodic flooding and exposure of coastal areas
CurrentsWind, tides and other forcesRedistribution of coastal sediments

How waves affect the shore

Most ordinary sea waves are generated when wind transfers energy to the water surface. Wave development depends mainly on wind speed, the duration of wind action and the distance over which the wind blows across uninterrupted water. This distance is called fetch.

As waves enter shallow coastal waters, interaction with the seabed slows them down. They become steeper and eventually break, releasing energy against the shore and disturbing sediments on the seabed.

Swash and backwash

  • Swash: Water moving up the beach after a wave breaks.
  • Backwash: Water returning down the beach towards the sea under gravity.

Both movements transport sediments. Their relative strength influences whether material accumulates on the beach or is removed from it.

Constructive and destructive waves

Constructive waves generally favour sediment accumulation because their swash is relatively stronger than their backwash. Destructive waves generally favour erosion because their backwash is relatively stronger and carries material away from the beach.

These terms describe the dominant effect of wave action. A beach may gain sediment during relatively calm conditions and lose sediment during storms.

Factors controlling coastal development

  • Energy and direction of waves.
  • Strength and direction of tidal and coastal currents.
  • Resistance, structure and arrangement of coastal rocks.
  • Availability of sand, gravel, silt and other sediments.
  • Shape and slope of the coast and adjoining seabed.
  • Changes in sea level and land elevation.

Waves are mainly movements of energy through water. Currents involve the directed movement of water, while tides are periodic variations in sea level accompanied by tidal currents.

Prelims focus

  • Wind is the principal cause of ordinary sea waves.
  • Fetch is the distance of uninterrupted water over which wind blows.
  • Swash moves towards the land; backwash returns towards the sea.
  • Constructive waves generally favour deposition.
  • Destructive waves generally favour erosion.
  • Trap: A tsunami is not an ordinary wind-generated wave or an astronomical tide.

[References: NCERT, Class 7, Our Environment, 2018-19 edition, Chapters 3 and 5, pp. 15-16 and 33-36; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Class 7, Social Science, 2021-22 English edition, Chapters 10-11, pp. 56-57 and 60-61; NCERT, Class 11, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Landforms and their Evolution, Waves and Currents section, SATHEE online edition; Newcastle University, Co-Curate, Longshore Drift. Online sources consulted on 28 November 2026; online textbook editions used where project PDF copies were unreadable or incomplete.]

title: Coastal Processes: Waves, Tides and Currents

body:
Mechanisms of marine erosion

When waves repeatedly strike a rocky coast, their energy gradually removes material from the shore. The rate of erosion depends on wave energy, rock resistance and the presence of joints, cracks and faults.

Principal mechanisms

  • Hydraulic action: The force of breaking waves and the compression of air and water within rock cracks loosen fragments.
  • Abrasion or corrasion: Sand, pebbles and other rock fragments carried by waves scrape and strike the coastal rocks.
  • Attrition: Rock fragments transported by waves collide with one another and become smaller and more rounded.
  • Solution or corrosion: Seawater dissolves susceptible minerals in certain rocks, contributing to their removal.

Abrasion wears away the coastal rock surface. Attrition wears down the fragments being transported.

Sea cliffs and wave-cut platforms

A sea cliff is a steep rock face along a coast. It develops where marine erosion, often assisted by weathering and slope failure, maintains a steep coastal slope.

The development of a sea cliff commonly follows this sequence:

  1. Breaking waves erode the lower part of a coastal rock face.
  2. Continued erosion creates an indentation called a wave-cut notch.
  3. The unsupported rock above the notch becomes unstable and collapses.
  4. Repeated undercutting and collapse cause the cliff to retreat inland.
  5. A gently sloping or nearly level rocky surface remains in front of the retreating cliff. This is called a wave-cut platform or wave-cut terrace.

A wave-cut platform is primarily erosional. It must be distinguished from a wave-built terrace, which develops through sediment accumulation.

Sea caves, arches, stacks and stumps

Waves concentrate their erosive action along weaknesses in coastal rocks, particularly on exposed headlands.

  1. Sea cave: Waves enlarge cracks and joints into cavities within a cliff or headland.
  2. Sea arch: Continued erosion may enlarge a cave or adjoining caves until an opening passes through the headland beneath a rock roof.
  3. Sea stack: When an arch roof collapses, an isolated pillar of rock may remain separated from the mainland.
  4. Sea stump: Continued erosion may reduce the stack to a low remnant near sea level.

This is a common developmental sequence, not a compulsory sequence through which every rocky coast must pass.

Headlands and bays

Where rocks of unequal resistance occur along a coastline, the less resistant sections are generally eroded more rapidly, producing indentations called bays. More resistant sections may remain projecting into the sea as headlands. This unequal removal of rock is called differential erosion.

As waves approach an irregular coast, parts of the same wave slow down at different rates because of differences in water depth. This bending of wave fronts is called wave refraction.

Wave energy commonly becomes concentrated around headlands and dispersed within sheltered bays. Consequently, exposed headlands often experience stronger erosion, while sheltered bays may favour sediment deposition and beach formation.

Prelims focus

  • Sea cliffs, wave-cut platforms, caves, arches and stacks are erosional features.
  • A wave-cut platform develops as a cliff retreats.
  • A sea stack is an isolated rock pillar.
  • Differential erosion commonly produces headlands and bays.
  • Wave refraction generally concentrates wave energy around headlands.
  • Trap: A wave-cut terrace is erosional, whereas a wave-built terrace is depositional.

[References: NCERT, Class 7, Our Environment, 2018-19 edition, Chapter 3, p. 16; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Class 7, Social Science, 2021-22 English edition, Chapter 10, pp. 56-57; NCERT, Class 11, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Landforms and their Evolution, Waves and Currents section; US National Park Service, Rocky Coast Landforms; BCcampus, Physical Geography Lab Manual, Lab 23: Coastal Geomorphology. Online sources consulted on 28 November 2026.]

title: Coastal Erosion: Cliffs, Caves, Arches and Stacks

body:
Conditions favouring deposition

Coastal deposition occurs where the energy of waves and currents becomes insufficient to transport all the available sediment. It is particularly common along sheltered bays and gently sloping coastal environments with an adequate sediment supply.

Coastal sediments may originate from rivers, eroding cliffs, previously deposited marine sediments and material transported from neighbouring shores.

Longshore drift

Longshore drift is the movement of sediment along a coastline under the influence of waves and associated coastal currents.

When waves approach a beach obliquely, the swash carries sediment diagonally up the beach. The backwash generally carries it directly down the slope under gravity. Repetition of these movements produces a net transfer of sediment along the shore.

Longshore drift is an important mechanism in the formation and development of beaches, spits and coastal bars. Its net direction may change when the prevailing direction of wave action changes.

Beaches and coastal dunes

A beach is an accumulation of loose sediment along a shore. Beaches commonly consist of sand, gravel, pebbles or a combination of these materials.

Beaches containing substantial quantities of rounded pebbles and coarse gravel are called shingle beaches. A beach does not necessarily consist of fine sand.

Dry sand from a beach may be transported inland by wind. Where wind velocity decreases or vegetation traps the moving sand, it accumulates into coastal sand dunes. Thus, although beaches are formed predominantly through marine deposition, coastal dunes are principally formed by wind deposition.

Bars, barriers and spits

Offshore bar and barrier bar

An offshore bar is an elongated ridge of sediment lying in nearshore waters, commonly approximately parallel to the coastline. It develops when waves and currents redistribute sediment and deposit it offshore.

When further accumulation builds the ridge above the water surface, it may form an exposed barrier bar. Such barriers can shelter the water and coastline behind them.

Spit

A spit is an elongated depositional feature attached to the mainland at one end and extending into the sea or across part of a bay or river mouth.

Longshore drift carries sediment along the coast. Where the coastline changes direction or a river mouth interrupts it, some of the transported material may accumulate and gradually extend into the water. Changes in wave direction can produce a curved or hooked end.

The sheltered area behind a spit may accumulate fine sediment and develop tidal mudflats or salt marshes.

Bay bar and lagoon

If sediment deposition extends a barrier across the entrance of a bay, the resulting feature may be called a bay bar. The body of water sheltered behind this barrier can develop into a lagoon.

A lagoon is separated from the open sea by a natural barrier, such as a sandbar, barrier island or reef. The separation may be partial, allowing seawater to enter through an inlet.

Continued sediment accumulation may gradually make a coastal lagoon shallower and, under suitable conditions, convert parts of it into marshes and coastal plains.

Tombolo

A tombolo is a ridge of deposited sediment that connects an offshore island or isolated rock feature to the mainland.

A lagoon is a water body created or enclosed by a natural barrier. The bar, barrier or spit separating it from the sea is the depositional landform.

Prelims focus

  • Longshore drift produces net sediment movement along the coast.
  • A beach may consist of sand, pebbles or gravel.
  • Coastal sand dunes are primarily formed by wind deposition.
  • A spit is attached to land at one end.
  • A tombolo connects an offshore feature to the mainland.
  • Trap: A lagoon need not be completely isolated from seawater.

[References: NCERT, Class 11, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Landforms and their Evolution, Depositional Landforms: Beaches and Dunes; Bars, Barriers and Spits; Newcastle University, Co-Curate, Longshore Drift; US National Park Service, Sandy Coast Landforms; NOAA National Ocean Service, What is a Lagoon? Online sources consulted on 28 November 2026.]

title: Coastal Deposition: Beaches, Bars, Spits and Lagoons

body:
Interaction between rivers and the sea

River mouths are transitional environments where freshwater, river-borne sediments, waves, tides and marine currents interact. The resulting landforms depend on the balance between sediment supplied by rivers and sediment redistributed by marine processes.

Formation of a delta

A delta is a low-lying accumulation of sediment formed at or near the mouth of a river where it enters a sea, lake or another body of relatively standing water.

When a river enters standing water, its flow generally spreads out and loses transporting capacity. Sediment begins to accumulate around the river mouth. If this accumulation exceeds removal by waves, currents and tides, the delta can grow.

Accumulating sediment may obstruct the main river channel and cause it to divide into several smaller channels called distributaries. Each distributary carries water and sediment towards the receiving water body.

Conditions favourable to delta development

  • An adequate and sustained supply of river-borne sediment.
  • Reduction in river transporting capacity near its mouth.
  • Marine processes that do not remove all deposited sediment.
  • Shallow adjoining waters that allow sediment accumulation to build land.

Although many deltas have a broadly triangular or fan-like appearance, delta shape varies according to river flow, waves, tides and sediment supply. A triangular shape is not essential to the definition of a delta.

Formation and characteristics of an estuary

An estuary is a partially enclosed coastal water body connected to the sea in which river water commonly mixes with seawater.

The mixture of freshwater and seawater is called brackish water. Its salinity varies according to river discharge, tides, rainfall and evaporation.

Estuaries can develop when rising relative sea level floods lower river valleys. They can also form in coastal depressions or where depositional barriers partly enclose a river mouth.

Strong tidal currents and marine sediment redistribution can prevent the development of an extensive delta at some river mouths. Nevertheless, estuaries can contain significant sediment deposits, including mudflats, sandbanks and marshes.

Distinguishing the 3 features

FeatureEssential characteristicTypical example
DeltaAccumulation of river-delivered sediment near a river mouthGodavari Delta
EstuaryCoastal water body where river water and seawater commonly mixNarmada Estuary
Coastal lagoonWater body separated from the open sea by a natural barrierChilika Lake

These features are not always mutually exclusive. A lagoon may receive river water and exhibit estuarine characteristics. A delta may contain estuarine channels, while sediment may accumulate within an estuary.

Identify a delta by sediment accumulation, an estuary by the river-sea transition, and a lagoon by the natural barrier separating its waters from the open sea.

Importance of coastal water bodies

Estuaries, lagoons and deltaic wetlands provide habitats for aquatic organisms, support fisheries and can reduce the impact of certain coastal hazards. However, their low elevation and dynamic sedimentary conditions also make them susceptible to flooding, erosion, sedimentation and changes in salinity.

Prelims focus

  • A delta develops when sediment accumulation exceeds removal.
  • Distributaries carry water away from the main river channel.
  • Brackish water is a mixture of freshwater and seawater.
  • The Narmada forms an estuary.
  • Chilika is a coastal lagoon.
  • Trap: Estuaries are not necessarily free of deposition, and deltas are not necessarily triangular.

[References: NCERT, Class 7, Our Environment, 2018-19 edition, Chapter 3, pp. 15-16; NCERT, Class 11, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Landforms and their Evolution, Deltas section; US Geological Survey, An Overview of Coastal Land Loss, Open File Report 03-337, Rivers and Deltas; NOAA National Ocean Service, Estuaries Tutorial, What is an Estuary? and Geology of Estuaries. Online sources consulted on 28 November 2026.]
